amendments.rule: An article that governs an **expressed** noun is not thereby barred from taking a nominal the ASV supplies inside its own phrase, and rule 22's *never the determiner* is not scoped to a substantival article. Where the ASV writes a determiner plus a supplied noun in front of the article's own noun, both words are the article's and the unit heads on the **supplied noun**: `τοῦ κυρίου` → *the kingdom* of gives the anaphoric nominal and the case preposition to the article and leaves `κυρίου` a bare *Lord* at REV.11.15, as `τῆς δόξης` → *the Lord* does, and as `τὴν … αἰώνιον` → *the life* does at 1JN.1.2, whose note records in terms that rule 49 does not reach an article governing an expressed head noun. Rule 60's closing clause already says the head follows the nominal wherever the article supplies one, `τῆς μελλούσης` → *that hour which* heading on *hour*; this rule is that clause holding for a supplied noun as well as a supplied determiner. The same holds where the article's complement is a **substantival adjective** and no noun is expressed at all: rule 49 gives the article both the determiner and the supplied noun, so `τὸν πτωχόν` → *the … man* and `τὰ ἐπιτήδεια` → *the things* and *needful* leave the adjective bare, headed on *man* and *things*. Rule 17's generic-noun clause is the contrast and is scoped to **anarthrous** Greek, where no article competes and the supplied noun is a rule 7 helper on the adjective — `πτωχός` → *a poor man* heads on *poor*, as rule 58's `νεκρῶν` → *the dead* and rule 51's anarthrous clause have it. So the test is whether a Greek article stands to take the determiner, exactly the test rules 51 and 58 already use. The corpus is unanimous: all fifty-three units of an article taking a determiner plus a nominal head on the nominal and none on *the*, and every unit finalized since rule 49 entered the contract reads the substantival-adjective shape the article's way, twelve to none. JAS.1.11 corrected this very head from *the* to *man* and JAS.1.25 repeats it, so do not read rule 17's unqualified wording as reaching a phrase an article governs. What the article takes is a **supplied** nominal, and rule 66's test is what identifies one: a word that completes the phrase and glosses no element of the adjective's own lexeme, as *man*, *part* and *things* do. Where the ASV instead renders the substantival adjective by a **multiword expression of its own**, every content word of which answers to that lexeme, no word of it is supplied and this rule has nothing to hand over: the article takes only the determiner, with any case preposition riding along under rule 21, and the whole expression stays with the adjective, headed under rule 66 on the word that glosses the lexeme rather than on the phrase's formal English head. `τῷ παραλυτικῷ` → *to the sick of the palsy* gives *to the* to the article and *sick of the palsy* to the adjective headed on *palsy*, as the same phrase does where the ASV writes *unto the sick of the palsy*. `ὁ κωφός` → *the … man* with a bare *dumb* is the contrast, *man* glossing no element of `κωφός`; and the anarthrous `παραλυτικόν` → *a man sick of the palsy* is rule 17's case, where no article competes and the completion stays with the adjective too. So ask of each English word whether it completes the phrase or renders the lexeme before handing any of it to the article, and never split one lexeme's own English between the article and the adjective in order to give the article a noun.
amendments.why: Rule 102's substantival-adjective clause is written for a supplied generic completion (*man*, *part*, *things*) and does not say what happens when the ASV renders the articular adjective by a multiword phrase that itself contains a noun. MAT.9 met that case three times: τῷ παραλυτικῷ → *to the sick of the palsy* at 9:2 and 9:6, against οἱ τυφλοί → *the … men* at 9:28 and ὁ κωφός → *the … man* at 9:33, which the same chapter reads the article's way. As it stood, a reader could hand *the … palsy* to the article and leave *sick of* to the adjective, splitting one lexeme's English across two units. The qualification imports rule 66's existing gloss-versus-completion test rather than inventing one, contradicts no corpus row (all fifty-three cited units are determiner-plus-generic-nominal, none a multiword lexeme gloss), and leaves rules 17, 49 and 58 untouched. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so that the over-broad sentence is corrected where it stands.

conventions: παραλυτικός → *sick of the palsy* heads on *palsy* in all three units (9:2 twice, 9:6). *sick* is the generic word and the phrase's formal English head only, which rule 17 forbids as a ground of choice; the chapter spends a bare *sick* on κακῶς at 9:12, and that is what shows under rule 91's operational test which word the ASV gives this lexeme.

An articular substantival adjective yields the supplied nominal to its article only where the ASV writes a generic completion: οἱ τυφλοί → *the … men* (9:28) and ὁ κωφός → *the … man* (9:33) give that noun to the article under rule 102 and leave the adjective bare. Where the ASV instead renders the adjective by a multiword expression of its own, τῷ παραλυτικῷ → *unto the sick of the palsy* (9:2) and *to the sick of the palsy* (9:6) give the article only the determiner with its case preposition and keep the whole expression on the adjective, no word of it being supplied. The anarthrous contrast is δύο τυφλοί → *two blind men* (9:27) and παραλυτικόν → *a man sick of the palsy* (9:2), where no article competes and rule 17 keeps the supplied noun in the adjective's own unit.

report: Checked all 52 candidate groups and, separately, the added/fold axis the lemma table is blind to. No construction in this chapter is analysed two ways without something in the source licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

Substantival adjectives, the closest call: οἱ τυφλοί (9:28) and ὁ κωφός (9:33) give the supplied nominal to the article under rule 102, while the anarthrous δύο τυφλοί (9:27) and παραλυτικόν (9:2) keep it in the adjective's own unit under rule 17's anarthrous clause. An article stands in the first pair and not in the second, which is the test rules 51, 58 and 102 already use.

The article table's T→A and T→V buckets each look like a split and are not: every treatment follows from what stands after the article — a name at 9:4 and 9:22 (rule 23), an expressed head noun before a participle at 9:8 (rule 31, corrected in that verse), a possessive at 9:1 and 9:14 (rules 20, 47), a written determiner at 9:2 and 9:6, a supplied nominal at 9:28 and 9:33 (rule 102), and no noun at all at 9:12 and 9:31 (rule 32).

Preverb particles are uniform: kept inside the compound verb's unit at 9:1, 9:9, 9:25, 9:26, 9:27, 9:31, 9:32, 9:33, 9:34, 9:35 and 9:38, and split off only at 9:15, where an expressed ἀπό writes its own 'from'. That is rule 106's 'in addition to' arm, not a second analysis. The oblique arm at 9:10 ('with Jesus' on the dative) and the accusative arm at 9:27 ('Have mercy on' with a bare 'us') likewise divide on case, as rule 106 requires.

παραλυτικός heads on 'palsy' in all three units (9:2 twice, 9:6). No corpus request was needed to settle it: the chapter itself spends a bare 'sick' on κακῶς at 9:12, so under rule 91's operational test 'sick' is not the word the ASV gives this lexeme, and rule 66's generic-completion arm reaches the same answer independently.

The two added units ('so did' at 9:19, 'that' at 9:30) and the folds at 9:13 ('this' on ἐστιν) and 9:31 ('fame' on διεφήμισαν) divide on rule 103's licensing test rather than on recurrence: ἠκολούθει is already spent on 'followed' at 9:19 and no source token carries the subordination at 9:30, while ἐστιν and διεφήμισαν are present and unspent. Consistent, and consistent with the thirteen participle-to-finite junctures placed under rule 88.

BSB: eleven disagreements, none a genuine error, and no edge was changed to improve the rate. Nine are articles the ASV leaves unrepresented because another word occupies the determiner slot (9:1 rule 47, 9:4, 9:6, 9:7, 9:20, 9:37 rule 20, 9:22 and 9:31 rule 38, 9:23 rules 20 and 57) — the documented convention difference.

The two non-article BSB rows: at 9:15 ἐφ᾽ ὅσον is three English words ('as long as'), so rule 94 forbids a compound unit and rule 34 empties the preposition, exactly as rule 94's own καθ᾽ ὑπερβολήν precedent does. At 9:18 εἷς is emptied by rule 58, the supplied 'a' belonging to the anarthrous ἄρχων, and the ASV's own gloss note 'Greek one ruler' corroborates that it wrote no word for the numeral.

Recorded two conventions and one amendment. Rule 102 as written says nothing about an articular substantival adjective whose ASV rendering is a multiword gloss containing a noun, and a reader could hand 'the … palsy' to the article at 9:6; the amendment closes that reading.
